title: Building Common Ground: The Tangram Task
text: Friday’s seminar, second hour · You just played the game. Now we analyse it: first in a corpus of 83 pairs who played what you played, then in 104 groups. Audiences change everything. Everything runs in RStudio on UCloud. Use your Methods01 procedure for setting up the running of the code.

title: Building Common Ground: The Tangram Task
text:
The question
An hour ago, describing a tangram took you a sentence. By round six, likely only two words did it, and your partner got faster at recognising the pictures. Yesterday’s lecture gave you Grice’s frame: say as much as is needed, no more, and what is needed tends to shrink as common ground grows.
But needed by whom? Today’s data lets us ask two different questions: what happens between two people building common ground (Hawkins, Frank & Goodman, 2020: 83 pairs, every message preserved), and what happens when the audience grows (Boyce, Hawkins, Goodman & Frank, 2024: the same game, groups of two to six).

title: Building Common Ground: The Tangram Task
text:
Learning Outcomes
By the end of this seminar, you will be able to:

Trace how referring expressions compress across repeated reference, in raw messages and in numbers.
Show that pairs say less while understanding more, and explain why that isn’t a paradox.
Compare experimental conditions: what does audience size do to compression and to understanding?
Match a measure to the right unit, and say why words-per-message and words-per-description can tell different stories.

title: Building Common Ground: The Tangram Task
text:
How it works
Same format as last week. Work with your partner from the game. Wherever you see ____, you write the code; everything comes from the last two Fridays, plus exactly one new ggplot move, introduced when you need it.
Start with Block 1 · The corpus.

title: 2 · The replication: two’s company
text: Block 3 · The same game, groups of two to six. Does common ground survive a crowd, and what does it cost to build?

title: 2 · The replication: two’s company
text:
Needed, by whom?
Grice’s speakers say as much as is needed. With one matcher, that’s one person’s common ground to track. Boyce, Hawkins, Goodman & Frank (2024) ran the exact game from Block 1 in groups of two to six: one describer, up to five matchers, everyone seeing the same twelve tangrams, six rounds. One description per trial has to work for the whole audience and each matcher only learns whether they themselves were right. 104 groups:







column
what it contains




group
which group ("group001" …)


group_size
how many players: 2, 3, 4, 5, or 6


trial · repetition · tangram
as before


message
one describer message


n_words
its length


n_correct
how many matchers picked right on this trial


n_matchers
how many matchers there were (group_size - 1)



 ⬇ multiparty_teaching.csv
multiparty <- read_csv("multiparty_teaching.csv")
glimpse(multiparty)

title: 2 · The replication: two’s company
section: Task 1: The measure has to match the unit
text:
Task 1: The measure has to match the unit
One wrinkle before any curve. Describers facing a crowd don’t type one long message; they split the description across several short ones, waiting for the stragglers. So mean(n_words) per message would hide exactly what we’re looking for. The unit of communication here is the trial, so first sum words within each trial, then average:
# Step 1: total describer words per trial.
per_trial <- multiparty %>%
  group_by(group, group_size, repetition, trial) %>%   # the unit: which column completes it?
  summarise(words = sum(n_words), .groups = "drop")

# Step 2: average trials, per group size and repetition.
red_multi <- per_trial %>%
  group_by(group_size, repetition) %>%
  summarise(mean_words = mean(words), .groups = "drop")

red_multi
# A tibble: 30 × 3  (your table - here as size x repetition)
repetition      2     3     4     5     6
1            21.7  23.2  27.3  27.3  24.9
2            15.8  15.9  18.2  25.9  17.5
3            10.7  13.0  14.1  15.4  18.1
4             8.2   8.8  11.5  13.3  13.4
5             5.7   6.1   9.1  10.2  11.3
6             5.2   6.0   6.6   6.8   7.3

title: 2 · The replication: two’s company
text:
Task 2: Five curves, one plot
The one new ggplot move of the day: colour = inside aes() draws one line per value of a variable; wrap the variable in factor() so R treats 2-6 as five categories, not a number line:
ggplot(red_multi, aes(x = repetition, y = mean_words,
                      colour = factor(group_size))) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  labs(title = "Everyone compresses, but crowds compress slightly less.",
       x = "repetition", y = "mean words per description",
       colour = "group size") +
  theme_bw()

Before you run it: all five curves will fall. What separates them; which sizes end up saying more at round six?

The bigger the audience, the longer the descriptions stay: 2-player groups reach ~5 words by round six, 6-player groups ~7, and the gap in the middle rounds is wider still. Shorthand for five people is slower to build than shorthand for one.

title: 2 · The replication: two’s company
section: Task 3: And what does the audience pay?
text:
Task 3: And what does the audience pay?
Accuracy needs one care-step: n_correct repeats on every message within a trial, so keep one row per trial first; distinct() does it (one new helper, self-explanatory):
multiparty %>%
  distinct(group, trial, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%     # one row per trial
  group_by(group_size, repetition) %>%
  summarise(pct_correct = 100 * mean(n_correct / n_matchers)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = repetition, y = pct_correct,
             colour = factor(group_size))) +
  geom_line() + geom_point() +
  labs(title = "Two reach ceiling. Six never do.",
       colour = "group size") +
  theme_bw()
% matchers correct, size x repetition:
repetition      2     3     4     5     6
1            82    83    84    78    80
2            89    87    88    84    85
6            97    91    87    83    86
Pairs end near 97%. Six-player groups plateau in the mid-80s, with longer descriptions. More words, less understanding, per listener.

title: 2 · The replication: two’s company
text:
Discuss with your neighbour
Why would five matchers make establishing common ground harder. The describer can’t tailor to anyone in particular, the matchers can’t all ask, feedback is private? And there is the Grice question underneath: when “as much as is needed” must satisfy five different common grounds at once, what is a speaker supposed to do: aim at the average, the slowest, or the room?

Where this leaves the theory. Reduction replicated at every size: the phenomenon is robust. But its rate depends on the audience: common ground builds through interaction, and interaction gets thinner as it’s shared five ways. “As much as is needed” turns out to have a hidden variable (needed by whom), and now you have a better grasp on it!

Done, or still curious? Open questions.

title: 1 · The corpus
text: Block 1 · Load the pair corpus, understand one row, and read one pair building shorthand in their own words.

title: 1 · The corpus
text:
83 pairs, playing your game
Stanford researchers had pairs of strangers play the Tangram game online (i.e., same twelve tangrams, director and matcher, six rounds, that you just played), but typed through a chat box, so every message survives (Hawkins, Frank & Goodman, 2020). Each row is one message:







column
what it contains




pair
which pair ("pair01" … "pair83")


trial
trial within the game (1–72)


repetition
which round this is for that tangram (1-6)


role
"director" or "matcher"


tangram
the target shape ("A" … "L")


message
what they typed


num_words
its length in words


correct
did the matcher pick right on this trial (1/0)

The shorthand builds up over rounds. Which column is the corpus’s clock (i.e., the one almost everything today gets grouped by)?

repetition: how many times the pair has met that tangram: 1 the first time, 6 the last. (trial just counts 1–72 through the game, all tangrams mixed.)

title: 1 · The corpus
text:
Read one pair first
Raw data before numbers, as always. Pair 1’s director, tangram B, all six rounds:
# One pair, one shape, six rounds.
tangrams %>%
  filter(pair == "pair01", role == "director", tangram == "B") %>%
  select(repetition, message)
# A tibble: 9 × 2
  repetition message
       <dbl> <chr>
1          1 this one kinda looks like they are looking a little down and kneeling with both arms out
2          1 wearing a dress maybe.
3          2 do not think we had this one
4          2 square head with diamond on right side
5          3 square triangle on side
6          3 like last time
7          4 square triangle on side forgot that one
8          5 square triangle head
9          6 triangle square head
Sixteen words become three. And notice rows 3 and 6: do not think we had this one, like last time: they’re managing what the two of them remember. The common ground is being mutually negotiated between them.






🤔 Think first



Look at what survived to round 6 (square, triangle, head) and what vanished (kinda looks like, maybe, this one). What is being compressed and what isn’t?






Check your thinking





What survives is what distinguishes this tangram from the other eleven. What vanishes is hedging and scaffolding: the apparatus of describing to someone who doesn’t know it yet. Once your partner knows it, the scaffolding is dead weight and removed (maxim of quantity, only convey what you need).





Your turn. Change one thing in the above code and follow tangram "L" instead. Does this exhibit the same progression?
Next: Exercise 1 — Less and less, better and better.

title: 4 · Finding an island
text: Block 3 · From how long the utterance is to what’s inside. We will have a look at how Anne’s WANT island develops through twelve months of speech.
crumbs: Workshop 1 · One Child, Word by Word

title: 4 · Finding an island
section: From how long to what’s inside
text:
From how long to what’s inside
MLU told you Anne’s utterances got longer but nothing about the content of her utterances. Time to look inside, and the reading tells you what to look for. On Tomasello’s account, a two-year-old doesn’t have “verbs” as a category: each verb is its own little island: a fixed part plus a slot, learned as a unit from use. Want + thing. More + thing.If that’s right, Anne’s speech should contain a pattern: the same frame, over and over, with different things dropped into the slot.
That’s a checkable claim, and checking it means collecting every “want” Anne ever produced and laying them side by side. For that, we need a new function.
crumbs: Workshop 1 · One Child, Word by Word

title: 4 · Finding an island
text:
str_detect()
str_detect(text, pattern) returns TRUE if the text contains the pattern. Wrap the pattern in \\b (word boundary) to match whole words only, and use (a|b) to match either of two words:
str_detect("want some juice", "\\bwant\\b")     # TRUE
str_detect("she wanted it",   "\\bwant\\b")     # FALSE - "wanted" is a different word
str_detect("wanna go",        "\\b(want|wanna)\\b")  # TRUE - matches either

What does str_detect("look at the snow", "no") return, without the \\b?

TRUE: s-no-w. Without boundaries the pattern matches anywhere, including inside other words. That’s what \\b is for.
crumbs: Workshop 1 · One Child, Word by Word

title: 4 · Finding an island
text:
The hunt
The str_detect() function slots straight into filter():
# Keep Anne's utterances containing "want" as a whole word.
want <- anne %>%
  filter(str_detect(utterance, "\\bwant\\b"))
  
# Anne's earliest wants (22 months):
want %>%
  filter(age_months == min(age_months)) %>%
  slice(1:15) %>%
  pull(utterance)
 [1] "want juice"           "want juice"           "want juice"           "want these"           "want toys"            "I want the shoes off"
 [7] "want water"           "want foot"            "want"                 "want more"            "want cupboard"        "want babys again"    
[13] "want prams"           "want prams"           "want prams" 
# And her latest wants (33 months):
want %>%
  filter(age_months == max(age_months)) %>%
  slice(1:15) %>%
  pull(utterance)
 [1] "I want black ones"                "want the red"                     "I think want cheese"              "I want my Mummy"                 
 [5] "um I don't want tea"              "want do another one now"          "which which one do you want"      "want this one"                   
 [9] "I want um"                        "we don't want the the dirty ones" "I don't want that"                "I don't want the rest out"       
[13] "don't want these ones in"         "we don't want them these ones"    "don't want them"  
Read the two sets side by side — early Anne runs one bare frame into the ground; late Anne is doing several new things at once. With your neighbour, find three concrete differences between the sets.






🤔 Think first



Got your three?






Check your thinking





The big ones: a subject has appeared in front of the verb (I want, we don’t want). At 22 months only one utterance out of these fifteen has it; by 33 it’s everywhere. Negation has arrived (don’t want), which barely exists early. And the slot has grown: from single nouns (juice, prams) to phrases (the red, the dirty ones) and even verbs (want do another one). One frame at 22 months; a small grammar around the verb by 33. You may also have caught I think want cheese and which one do you want: the island getting embedded in bigger structures.
crumbs: Workshop 1 · One Child, Word by Word

title: 4 · Finding an island
text:
How does the island develop?
You just found the differences by reading fifteen utterances at each end. But two snapshots can’t show how the change happened: was it gradual, or sudden? For that you need every month in between, and a way to turn one of your observations into a number.
Take the first one: the subject. It’s ideal to count: an utterance either has I before its want or it doesn’t. For each month, we can ask: of Anne’s wants, what share carry the subject?
# Of Anne's wants, per month: what share carry the subject?
iwant_anne <- want %>%
  mutate(with_subject = str_detect(utterance, "\\bI want\\b")) %>%
  group_by(age_months) %>%
  summarise(subject_share = 100 * mean(with_subject),
            n_wants = n())

ggplot(iwant_anne, aes(x = age_months, y = subject_share)) +
  geom_line(colour = "grey50") +
  geom_point(aes(size = n_wants), alpha = .4) +
  labs(title = "Anne's WANT island grows a subject",
       x = "age (months)", y = "% of wants with 'I'",
       size = "wants that month") +
  theme_bw()
Look at the shape and at the dots: they’re sized by how many wants Anne produced that month, because a share computed from twenty utterances deserves less trust than one computed from two hundred. Do you see any convincing patterns in the data?
crumbs: Workshop 1 · One Child, Word by Word

title: 4 · Finding an island
text:
And the other eleven?
One child, one trajectory. But the reading makes a bet about all children. One plot would allow more insight: same pipeline, started from the full table, one panel per child:
# Of each child's wants, per month: what share carry the subject?
iwant_growth <- manchester %>%
  filter(speaker == "CHI") %>%
  mutate(has_want = str_detect(utterance, "\\b(want)\\b")) %>%
  filter(has_want) %>%
  mutate(with_subject = str_detect(utterance, "\\bI (want)\\b")) %>%
  group_by(child, age_months) %>%
  summarise(subject_share = 100 * mean(with_subject),
            n_wants = n(),
            .groups = "drop")

ggplot(iwant_growth, aes(x = age_months, y = subject_share)) +
  geom_line(colour = "grey50") +
  geom_point(aes(size = n_wants), alpha = .4) +
  facet_wrap(~child) +
  labs(title = "Twelve islands grow a subject, one child per panel",
       x = "age (months)", y = "% of wants with 'I'",
       size = "wants that month") +
       theme_bw()
Discuss with your neighbour. First describe what you see: are there any clear patterns? Is there one answer for all twelve, or one per panel? Then take Becky: 79% one month, 15% a few months later, back up to 70%. Did her grammar un-develop? If not, what is that sawing, and is it a problem for the theory or for the measurement?
crumbs: Workshop 1 · One Child, Word by Word

title: 4 · Finding an island
text:
Make the call on “Wanna”
Are these plots a problem for the theory or for the measurement? Let’s inspect our assumptions about measurement. Every count on this page used the pattern \\bwant\\b, but Anne also says wanna. Is wanna + verb part of the same island as want + thing, or a different construction? That’s a theoretical question! Let’s get some more data and read her wanna utterances:
# All of Anne's wanna-utterances.
anne %>%
  filter(str_detect(utterance, "____")) %>%
  pull(utterance)
[1] "I wanna know in that pot"                  "wanna sleeping with Mummy"                 "wanna lie down"                           
  [4] "they wanna go on here"                     "I wanna play"                              "I wanna play"                             
  [7] "I wanna play my sand"                      "I wanna go in the kitchen"                 "wanna come with you and your mummie"      
 [10] "I wanna see"                               "I wanna wanna have tea"                    "wanna sit there"                          
 [13] "wanna play games"                          "wanna play"                                "I wanna see"                              
 [16] "I wanna go in there"                       "don't wanna"                               "don't wanna"                              
 [19] "don't wanna"                               "wanna go in here"                          "me wanna do it"                           
 [22] "wanna put a video on"                      "wanna push it on"                          "wanna go nursery" 
 ...






🤔 Think first



What would Tomasello say?






Check your thinking





He’d note they have different frames: want + thing, wanna + verb, and on his account, different frames are different constructions, possibly not yet connected in Anne’s head. So excluding is defensible. But so is including, if your question is “how often does Anne express wanting?” What you count depends on what you’re asking.





Your turn. Take the twelve-panel chunk above and add wanna to both patterns: the filter() and the with_subject line. Rerun. Does the inclusive ruling change our main results?
Done, or are you still curious? How do other verbs develop over time? You can have a look here:
Next: Exercise 2 — Does the island grow?.

title: 2 · Meet one child properly
text:
One child: Anne
We’ll first follow Anne. First step: keep only her rows, and only what she said.
# Keep Anne's own utterances: her recordings, her speech.
anne <- manchester %>%
  filter(child == "Anne", speaker == "CHI")
Select the lines and press Shift+Enter. Nothing prints. The result went into the variable anne. Check what you got:
# How many utterances, over which ages?
anne %>%
  count(file)
> anne %>% count(age_months)
# A tibble: 12 × 2
   age_months     n
        <dbl> <int>
 1         22  1122
 2         23  2568
 3         24  1968
 4         25  1782
 5         26  1154
 6         27  1727
 7         28  2047
 8         29  1922
 9         30  1088
10         31  3057
11         32  1024
12         33  1286
Every row of this little table refers to Anne at that age, saying that many utterances.

Suppose you had typed filter(child == "Anne", speaker == "MOT") instead. How many of the rows would be Anne herself talking?

0: that filter keeps the mother’s utterances from Anne’s recordings. Both filters matter: child picks the recordings, speaker picks the voice.



Anne’s ages are given in months, but each row also records which recording file it came from. Which table will have more rows: anne %>% count(age_months) or anne %>% count(file)? Write the code and figure it out!

count(file): Anne was recorded about twice every three weeks, so most months contain two recordings, sometimes three. Run both and compare: twelve months, but many more files. Everything we compute today groups by month, which quietly bundles those sessions together — a big month is often just a double month. Keep that in mind when a number looks surprisingly high or low.

title: 2 · Meet one child properly
section: Let’s have a look at the raw data!
text:
Let’s have a look at the raw data!
Statistics come later. Start the way you’d start with any new dataset: look at the raw data. Here is Anne at her youngest:
# Anne's utterances from her very first recording.
anne %>%
  filter(age_months == min(age_months)) %>% # keep only her earliest month (minimum number in age_months)
  slice(1:25) %>% # rows 1 to 25 (R counts from 1!)
  pull(utterance) # just this column, as plain text
Two of the lines are new. slice(1:25) keeps rows 1 to 25, like indexing in Python, except R counts from 1, not 0. pull(utterance) takes just that one column out of the table, so the console shows you plain text instead of a tibble.
 [1] "baby"            "it"              "it fit"          "push push push"  "Anne"            "what's that"     "what's that"    
 [8] "baby baby Mummy" "car"             "hair"            "what's that"     "train"           "choo o"          "big"            
[15] "tip"             "tip"             "spider"          "spider"          "what's that"     "piggy"           "what's that"    
[22] "a cake"          "what's that"     "look"            "teddy"
Read them. This is a real two-year-old, mid-play, mid-lunch. Your turn. Copy the chunk above and change one thing so it shows the recording at her oldest age in the dataset instead.






🤔 Think first



Which one thing?






Check your thinking





min becomes max. Everything else stays: the pipeline logic (i.e., filter to one session, take some rows, pull the text) is unchanged; only which session you’re pointing at differs.

title: One Child, Word by Word
text:
The question
How does a child get from single words to grammar?
This week’s reading gives you Tomasello’s answer: not all at once, and not as a system. Each verb starts out as its own island, its own little construction, with its own frame learned from use (want + thing; more + thing). Grammar, on this account, is what emerges as the islands grow and connect. It’s a radical claim, because the traditional picture (i.e., Chomsky’s) says grammatical knowledge is general from the start, not built verb by verb.
Radical claims need evidence, and this one makes a checkable prediction: a two-year-old’s verbs should be uneven: some flexible, some frozen, each on its own schedule. Today you check it, on the corpus that was collected to check it: you’ll follow Anne from her second birthday toward her third, watch one island grow, and then ask whether what you found holds across eleven more children.
crumbs: Workshop 1 · One Child, Word by Word

title: One Child, Word by Word
text:
Learning Outcomes
By the end of this seminar, you will be able to:

Load a real corpus into R and say precisely what one row of it means
Compute and plot a developmental measure (MLU) and read its dips without over-reading them
Hunt a construction through twelve months of child speech with str_detect(), and defend what you chose to count
Compare development across twelve children, and say what one child’s data can and cannot show
Tell the difference between a noisy point and a finding, using the n it rests on

title: 1 · Meet the data
text:
Twelve children learning to talk
Between 1998 and 2001, researchers in Manchester recorded twelve English children at home, playing and talking with their mothers: an hour at a time, twice in every three-week period, from around each child’s second birthday until around their third. The children are known by first names: Anne, Aran, Becky, Carl, Dominic, Gail, Joel, John, Liz, Nicole, Ruth and Warren.
This is the Manchester corpus (Theakston, Lieven, Pine & Rowland, 2001). It was collected to test the theory you read this week: that children build grammar verb by verb, and it is publicly available through CHILDES, the international database of child language.
Everything the children and mothers said was transcribed. We have converted those transcripts into one table, where each row is one utterance: one thing one person said at one moment.







column
what it contains




child
which child’s recording this is ("Anne", "Becky", …)


age_months
the child’s age at that recording, in months


speaker
who is talking: "CHI" (the child) or "MOT" (the mother)


utterance
what they said


num_tokens
how many words that is



So the row Anne · 26 · CHI · "want some juice" · 3 means: Anne, aged 2;2, said want some juice: three words.

The mothers talk a lot in these recordings. Which column would you use to keep only the children’s utterances?

speaker: filtering for speaker == "CHI" keeps the child’s own speech. child tells you whose recording it is; even in Anne’s files, half the rows are her mother.
crumbs: Workshop 1 · One Child, Word by Word

title: 1 · Meet the data
text:
Download the data
 ⬇ manchester_utterances.rds
This is an .rds file: R’s own format for saving a data frame exactly as it is, types and all. Download it, then upload it into your working folder on UCloud: drag it into the Files pane, or use the Upload button there.

title: 1 · Meet the data
text:
Load it
# Load the tidyverse.
library(tidyverse)

# Read the data file into a variable called manchester.
manchester <- readRDS("manchester_utterances.rds")
Select the lines and press Shift+Enter. If R complains that the file does not exist, the file and your session are in different folders. Check the Files pane.
Now have a first look:
# glimpse() shows every column, its type, and the first few values.
glimpse(manchester)
Rows: 597,644
Columns: 6
$ child      <chr> "Anne", "Anne", "Anne", "Anne", "Anne", "Anne", "Anne", "Anne", "Anne", "Anne", "Anne", "Anne", "Anne", "Anne", "Anne", "Anne…
$ file       <chr> "011007", "011007", "011007", "011007", "011007", "011007", "011007", "011007", "011007", "011007", "011007", "011007", "0110…
$ age_months <dbl> 22, 22, 22, 22, 22, 22, 22, 22, 22, 22, 22, 22, 22, 22, 22, 22, 22, 22, 22, 22, 22, 22, 22, 22, 22, 22, 22, 22, 22, 22, 22, 2…
$ speaker    <chr> "CHI", "MOT", "CHI", "CHI", "MOT", "MOT", "MOT", "MOT", "MOT", "MOT", "MOT", "MOT", "MOT", "MOT", "MOT", "MOT", "CHI", "MOT",…
$ utterance  <chr> "baby", "here's baby", "it", "it fit", "baby willn't fit", "is it too big", "what about this baby look", "wanna put them on t…
$ num_tokens <int> 1, 2, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 6, 3, 4, 3, 3, 3, 3, 3, 3, 1, 3, 1, 3, 2, 2, 2, 2, 6, 3, 2, 1, 6, 7, 5, 1, 2, 4, 2, 1, 2, 2, 8, 9, 3,…
Note the types: <chr> means text, <int> means whole numbers. speaker and utterance are text; age_months and num_tokens are numbers you can compute with.






🤔 Think first



num_tokens says how many words an utterance has. Someone had to decide what a word is. Does don’t count as one word or two? Does a laugh count? Last Friday you made decisions exactly like this about turns.






Check your thinking





There is no neutral answer. Our rule: anything separated by spaces is a word, so don’t is one, and laughs and unintelligible stretches don’t count at all. Different rules would give different numbers in everything you compute today. That’s how measurement works.

The totals differ a lot between children. And one thing to know about age_months: because ages are rounded to the month, a busy month can contain two recording sessions bundled together. Raw counts reflect the recording schedule as much as the child. Keep that in mind; it will matter when we start comparing sessions.

title: Mean Length of Utterance
text: Block 2 · Compute Anne’s mean length of utterance, plot it, and test it against your observations from the raw data.
crumbs: Workshop 1 · One Child, Word by Word

title: Mean Length of Utterance
text:
The measure
Mean Length of Utterance (MLU): the average number of words per utterance. It sounds almost too simple, and yet since Brown (1973) it has been the standard yardstick of early grammar, for a good reason: to say longer things, you have to combine more things. A child at MLU 1.5 is mostly naming; a child at MLU 3.5 is building sentences. You already have everything you need: num_tokens holds each utterance’s length, and age_months groups utterances into months of recording.
crumbs: Workshop 1 · One Child, Word by Word

title: Mean Length of Utterance
text:
Task 1: MLU per month
For every month, compute the mean of num_tokens and count how many utterances that mean is based on.
# For each month: Anne's average utterance length, and how much data it rests on.
mlu_anne <- anne %>%
  group_by(____) %>%
  summarise(mlu = mean(____),
            n_utts = n())

# Look at the result.
mlu_anne
# A tibble: 12 × 3
   age_months   mlu n_utts
        <dbl> <dbl>  <int>
 1         22  1.57   1122
 2         23  1.70   2568
 3         24  1.86   1968
 4         25  2.20   1782
 5         26  2.49   1154
 6         27  2.60   1727
 7         28  2.43   2047
 8         29  2.46   1922
 9         30  2.61   1088
10         31  2.68   3057
11         32  2.52   1024
12         33  2.85   1286






Hint





Which column defines a month of recording? Which column holds the utterance lengths? Both are shown in the table on the data page.
crumbs: Workshop 1 · One Child, Word by Word

title: Mean Length of Utterance
text:
Task 2: Plot it
Before plotting, one prediction. Bring back Anne’s utterances from her oldest age (you built this on the last page):
# Anne's utterances at her oldest:eyeball their lengths.
anne %>%
  filter(age_months == max(age_months)) %>%
  slice(1:25) %>%
  pull(utterance)

Look at those 25 utterances: some long, plenty short. If you averaged their lengths, roughly where would it land? That’s your prediction for where the curve ends at 33 months.

Just under 3. If you guessed higher, look again at how many one- and two-word turns sit between the long ones: yeah, no, there. The mean drags every short reply along with the impressively long sentences. The plot shows how she gets there from ~1.5: how fast, and how smoothly.


# Plot MLU against age.
ggplot(mlu_anne, aes(x = ____, y = ____)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line() +
  labs(title = "Anne's mean length of utterance",
       x = "age (months)", y = "MLU (words)") +
  theme_bw()
Run it. You should see a line with one point per month, starting near where you read Anne naming things and ending near where you read her building sentences.
crumbs: Workshop 1 · One Child, Word by Word

title: Mean Length of Utterance
text:
Task 3: Read the plot
With your partner:
1 · The verdict on your sentence. On the last page you wrote one sentence about what changed between Anne’s first and last recordings. Does the curve agree with you? And is there anything you noticed by looking at her data that a per-month average could never show?
2 · Find a dip. Somewhere the curve drops from one month to the next. Is Anne’s language deteriorating here?






🤔 Think first



Before you answer. Look at n_utts across the months. Some months have roughly double the utterances of others. Why?






Check your thinking





Anne was recorded about twice every three weeks, but our ages are rounded to the month, so some months contain two recording sessions bundled together, and some just one. A mean over 1,000 utterances is steadier than a mean over 500; and a single session catches a single day’s mood, sleep, and lunch. We’ll see later on how we can represent this in a plot.





In Task 1, you computed MLU per month for Anne. The same pipeline computes it for all twelve children at once: the only change is where you start, and what you group by:
# MLU per month, for every child: start from the FULL table this time.
mlu_all <- ____ %>%                       # not anne - which table has everyone?
  filter(speaker == "CHI") %>%
  group_by(child, ____) %>%               # group by child AND month
  summarise(mlu = mean(num_tokens),
            .groups = "drop")

mlu_all
Grouping by two columns gives one row per child per month. Twelve growth curves in one table. (.groups = "drop" just tells R to hand back a plain table afterwards; without it you get a harmless warning.)
crumbs: Workshop 1 · One Child, Word by Word

title: Mean Length of Utterance
section: Task 4: All twelve children at once
text:
Task 4: All twelve children at once
Twelve lines, one picture. Two new ggplot moves, both small: group = child draws one line per child instead of connecting everything into spaghetti, and a second geom_line() with its own data = draws Anne again, on top, in colour:
ggplot(mlu_all, aes(x = age_months, y = mlu, group = child)) +
  geom_line(colour = "grey70") +
  geom_line(data = mlu_all %>% filter(child == "Anne"), colour = "firebrick", linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(title = "Anne among the twelve",
       x = "age (months)", y = "MLU (words)") +
  theme_bw()

Interpret the plot
With your partner, discuss the following: How much do twelve normally-developing children differ at the same age? Find the widest vertical spread. How many months of development does that gap correspond to along the curve?






One honest limit



MLU says Anne’s and the other children’s utterances got longer, but it says nothing about what’s in them. Want some juice and Mummy sock fall both score three words, but they are very different achievements. Same number, different grammar. Next block, we look inside the utterances themselves.


Curve made and argued about? Next: Finding an island.

title: 6 · Open questions
text: If you’re interested, every question below can be tackled with the tools you used today; and not everything below has a known answer!
crumbs: Workshop 1 · One Child, Word by Word

title: 6 · Open questions
text:
1 · The second island
Everything today was WANT. Pick another verb (e.g., have, like, get, put) and give it the full treatment: read early and late hits, then plot its subject-share across the twelve children.
The question that makes this interesting: within one child, do the two islands grow their subject at the same time? If grammar is one system, they should move together. If each island grows from its own use, WANT might have a subject months before LIKE does. Nobody knows the answer, yet!
crumbs: Workshop 1 · One Child, Word by Word

title: 6 · Open questions
text:
2 · The Warren problem
Have a look at Warren’s panel of word islands. It starts near 70%, meaning that he uses the subject already at 22 months, before Anne’s has begun. Is this precocious grammar, or one frozen chunk? Try to read his early I wants. If the slot varies (I want juice, I want teddy, I want down), the frame is productive. If it’s the same phrase on repeat, it’s a formula wearing a subject. Figure out what’s going on with Warren by looking at the data.
crumbs: Workshop 1 · One Child, Word by Word

title: 6 · Open questions
text:
3 · The error nobody taught
Children say things no adult ever said to them: goed, comed, falled, foots, mouses. These are the classic evidence that children build rules rather than copy. You can’t imitate what nobody says.
Try to detect them: "\\b(goed|comed|falled|breaked|foots|mouses|sheeps)\\b" and extend the net with your own guesses. Which children produce them, and at what ages? And then check the mothers. If an error truly has a frequency of zero in the input, what does its existence tell you, and can either theory claim it?
crumbs: Workshop 1 · One Child, Word by Word

title: 6 · Open questions
text:
4 · What’s that → what’s what?
Questions have their own development: what and where come early; why, famously, arrives late and then detonates. Track the four question words: what, where, who, why per 100 utterances across age, for a child of your choice. When does why explode? And is the explosion a language fact or a cognition fact. What does a child need to understand before why is worth asking?
crumbs: Workshop 1 · One Child, Word by Word

title: Exercise 1 · Less and less, better and better
text: Block 2 · Measure the compression across all 83 pairs, check what it cost, and see what the common ground became.

title: Exercise 1 · Less and less, better and better
text:
Task 1: The two curves
Pair 1 went from sixteen words to three. Rule or habit? And what did the matchers pay for it? Two pipelines, same shape:
# For each repetition: average director message length.
reduction <- tangrams %>%
  filter(role == "____") %>%
  group_by(____) %>% # Which variable are we interested in seeing the progression over here?
  summarise(mean_words = mean(____))

reduction

# For each repetition: how often the matcher picked right.
accuracy <- tangrams %>%
  group_by(repetition) %>%
  summarise(pct_correct = 100 * mean(____))

accuracy
# A tibble: 6 × 2
  repetition mean_words
       <dbl>      <dbl>
1          1        9.6
2          2        7.0
3          3        5.2
4          4        4.0
5          5        3.6
6          6        3.2

# A tibble: 6 × 2
  repetition pct_correct
       <dbl>       <dbl>
1          1          78
2          2          85
3          3          91
4          4          92
5          5          95
6          6          95

Before you looked: directors say three times less by round six. What did you expect accuracy to do, and what does it actually do?

It rises: 78% to 95%. Less said, more understood. Grice’s maxim of quantity (i.e., as much as is needed) has a moving target in this experiment: what’s needed shrinks as common ground grows. The words that disappeared had become redundant for this pair.


Try to plot both repetition on x, the measure on y, geom_point() + geom_line(). Two plots, four blanks, no help needed by now.
crumbs: Exercise 1: Less and less, better and better

title: Exercise 1 · Less and less, better and better
section: Task 2: For this pair and no other
text:
Task 2: For this pair and no other
For this pair. Here’s what tangram B ended up being called, across pairs, in round six:
# Final-round names for tangram B.
tangrams %>%
  filter(role == "director", repetition == 6, tangram == "B") %>%
  select(pair, message) %>%
  slice(1:12)
   pair    message
 1 pair01  triangle square head
 2 pair02  mountain praying
 3 pair03  hand is only a triangle to the right side
 4 pair04  kneeling tilted head
 5 pair05  angel praying
 6 pair06  on knees feet in back pointed down head bent next to triangle
 7 pair07  arms wide
 8 pair08  box being held up by triangle on the right
 9 pair09  split triangle
10 pair10  praying monk
11 pair11  mouse
12 pair12  kneel arms right and left
One shape: triangle square head, angel praying, arms wide, mouse. Every pair compressed onto its own name, grown from its own first description. Drop pair 10’s matcher into pair 11 and mouse means nothing. Conventions are local to the dyad in communication!
Hedges (looks like, kinda, maybe, sort of) are the grammar of not-yet-knowing-together. Count their disappearance:
tangrams %>%
  filter(role == "director") %>%
  mutate(hedged = str_detect(message, "looks like|kinda|maybe|sort of")) %>%    # the net, alternatives joined by |
  group_by(repetition) %>%
  summarise(pct_hedged = 100 * mean(hedged, na.rm = TRUE))
# A tibble: 6 × 2
  repetition pct_hedged
       <dbl>      <dbl>
1          1         29
2          2          9
3          3          3
4          4          1
5          5          1
6          6          0
Twenty-nine percent to zero. Widen the net (I think, possibly, seems) and check the story survives your ruling.

So far: between two people, common ground grows, words fall, hedges vanish, understanding climbs, and the expression that remains is a private language. Next block: what does having an audience do to the task?

Next: The replication: two’s company.

title: 3 · Open questions
text: If you’re ahead, you can explore the following questions. Not everything here has a known answer.

title: 3 · Open questions
text:
1 · The matcher goes quiet
In the pair corpus, filter role == "matcher" and track their messages per repetition: how many, and how many containing "\\?". They nearly vanish by round six. So who built the shorthand: the one who shortened, or the one who stopped needing to ask? And in the multiparty data the matchers couldn’t all ask: is that exactly why the crowds stayed wordy?

title: 3 · Open questions
text:
2 · Do crowds invent different names?
Pair-built names got weird: mouse, angel praying. A name for five people has to work for five first-impressions at once. Pull round-6 descriptions for one tangram from the 2-player and the 6-player groups and read them side by side: are crowd names more literal? More square-triangle-head? Less mouse?

title: 3 · Open questions
text:
3 · Does shorthand transfer?
Pair 11’s mouse would baffle pair 10. But a matcher from a 6-player group has heard descriptions built for a crowd. Would they fare better with a stranger’s names? Wilkes-Gibbs & Clark (1992) swapped listeners mid-game to test this in pairs; design the group version: measure, prediction, and the result that would surprise you.

title: 3 · Open questions
text:
4 · Invent the measure
Hedges vanished in pairs. Pick something else that marks not-yet-knowing-together: pointing language (this one), questions from the describer, politeness, and track it in both datasets: does it fade faster with one matcher than with five?
